solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Area partly covered by London legislation to the west? (5)

definitions.text: Area partly covered by London legislation to the west?

indicators.note: in an across clue west is leftward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: SE, the South East, a region that takes in part of London

explanation.surface: A question about which lands to the west are subject to laws made in London.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also defines the answer: Wales lies west of London and only some of its laws are made at Westminster, the rest being devolved to its own parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Wales is a region west of London where Westminster legislation applies only in part.

clue.text: Suspect Bard wore every costume (8)

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means not to be trusted, so the letters are not in their proper order

explanation.surface: An accusation that Shakespeare dressed up in every outfit going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' looks like a verb in a whodunnit about the Bard; it is an adjective telling you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre's wardrobe is its entire stock of costumes.

clue.text: Enter details of account’s brand name (3,2)

blocks.note: a logo is a brand's emblem

explanation.surface: Filling in a form with the trading name of a business account.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to 'account': to log on is to enter your account details. The 's stands for 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Logging on means typing in the username and password for your account.

clue.text: Drunk now, like it or not (2,5)

blocks.note: here = now, as in 'the moment is here'

explanation.surface: Someone announcing they are drunk, and you can take it or leave it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' reads as an adjective, but it is the noun: a drunk, a SOT.
explanation.definitionFit: 'So there!' is said to close an argument, meaning you will have to accept it whether you like it or not.

clue.text: Poorly rated deputy ready to be fired (8)

blocks.note: a sub is a substitute or deputy
a primed gun is ready to fire

explanation.surface: A deputy with bad reviews who is about to get the sack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' suggests dismissal from a job; it is the gun sense, where priming comes before firing.
explanation.definitionFit: Subprime loans or borrowers have a poor credit rating.

clue.text: From attempt to catch salmon, maybe bears suffer cold (11)

indicators.note: in a down clue, the part that bears another sits beneath it, so OF FISH goes under STAND

blocks.note: of = from, as in 'a man of Kent'
to fish is to try to catch fish, salmon being one

explanation.surface: Bears catching salmon, and suffering in the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a wildlife scene with bears fishing; 'bears' is only placing one piece under another.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for an aloof manner: someone who keeps others at arm's length is cold in the social sense.

clue.text: Later acquisition noted by auditor (3)

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so this is what the ear takes in

blocks.note: a buy is a purchase, an acquisition

explanation.surface: An accountant spotting a purchase made after the books closed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' pretends to be an accountant; here it is simply a listener. 'Later' is the casual goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Later!' and 'bye!' are both casual ways of saying goodbye.

clue.text: Funny comic perhaps uncovered her ferret (7)

indicators.note: her with its outer letters stripped off

blocks.note: a comic is one kind of magazine, or mag
HER without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A strange tale of a comedian meddling with a woman's pet ferret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ferret' is the verb, to hunt about, not the animal; 'comic' is a paper, not a comedian.
explanation.definitionFit: To ferret about is to rummage, searching through things.

clue.text: Male genes modified to limit alpha element (9)

indicators.note: changed, so the letters of genes are rearranged
the rearranged genes enclose the A, keeping it within bounds

blocks.note: rearranged to go round the A
alpha is A in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Genetic engineering on men to restrict some alpha element in them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Male' supplies MAN, not just M, and the rearranged GENES take the A inside: G(A)NESE.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: this metal, number 25 in the periodic table, is one of the chemical elements.

clue.text: Broad spiral rotating part of every galaxy (4)

indicators.note: turning round, so the letters read backwards
the answer is a piece of the following words

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of every and the start of galaxy

explanation.surface: A description of a spiral galaxy wheeling around.
explanation.walkthrough: The astronomy is all surface; the answer sits backwards across 'every galaxy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gyre is a large spiral or circular motion, like an ocean gyre.

clue.text: Leaders muddled in battle rush order to reorient troops (5,4)

indicators.note: the first letters of the two words get swapped

blocks.note: fight = battle; it takes the R from the second word
race = rush; it takes the F from the first word

explanation.surface: Confused officers rushing into battle and barking orders to turn the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' looks like army commanders; it means the front letters of the words.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Right face!' is the drill command to turn ninety degrees to the right.

clue.text: Lolly somebody coated with crumbs! (5)

indicators.note: one word covers the other on the outside

blocks.note: crumbs! and my! are both mild exclamations

explanation.surface: An ice lolly dropped and covered in crumbs.
explanation.walkthrough: Lolly is British slang for money, and also an ice lolly, which is where the crumbs come from.
explanation.definitionFit: Lolly is informal British slang for money.

clue.text: Nothing left of citrus drops, everything sold (5)

indicators.note: the citrus fruit lets go of a letter

blocks.note: an orange is a citrus fruit
O (nothing) at the left end is removed

explanation.surface: A market stall down to its last citrus fruit after selling out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Citrus drops' sounds like boiled sweets; it is the orange losing its O.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop's range is its whole selection of goods for sale.

clue.text: See one box splits quite apart (9)

indicators.note: the inserted letters break DATE in two

blocks.note: to see someone is to date them

explanation.surface: A single box being split wide open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is the romantic sense, going out with someone, and 'splits' puts the other two pieces inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Disparate things are wholly different, quite apart from each other.

clue.text: Exchange of shots after sit-ins exploited by the left (11)

indicators.note: used for another purpose, so the letters are reworked
the rally comes after the rearranged letters

blocks.note: a rally is an exchange of shots in tennis

explanation.surface: Violence breaking out after left-wing protesters staged sit-ins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exchange of shots' suggests gunfire; it is a tennis rally. 'The left' feels political but is just the side.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinistrally means on or towards the left, from Latin sinister, left.

clue.text: Bachelor say, if gender reassigned, probably missing balls? (14)

indicators.note: the letters are given new places

explanation.surface: A crude joke about a bachelor who has changed gender and so lacks certain body parts.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's balls are anatomical; the definition's balls are the ones a clumsy fielder fails to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: A butterfingered person tends to drop things, so is likely to miss catches.

clue.text: Decent plain rounds within compass of bell-ringer, nearly (9)

indicators.note: turns round, so BARE runs backwards
inside the bounds of the next word
the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: TOLLER, one who tolls a bell, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A modest description of the plain rounds that bell-ringers chime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' and 'rounds' are both change-ringing terms, which is the disguise: plain here is simply bare, and rounds tells you to turn it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerable means acceptable, decent enough.

clue.text: A certain stage not available to North Hollywood resident? (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

blocks.note: one = a certain, as in 'one Mr Smith'
a leg is a stage of a journey or race

explanation.surface: A question about a theatre stage off limits to someone in North Hollywood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North Hollywood' reads as the Los Angeles district, but North is the reversal instruction. The question mark flags that Hollywood is only one example of Los Angeles.
explanation.definitionFit: An Angeleno is a native or resident of Los Angeles, which includes Hollywood.

clue.text: Grafter losing in photo finish for medals, pressure showing (7,7)

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the word for losing goes within the word for photo
the last letter of the next word

blocks.note: a film that's on is showing

explanation.surface: An athlete who worked hard losing a photo finish for medals under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grafter' looks like a hard worker, but it is someone who grafts skin. 'Photo finish' is not a phrase here: 'losing' is split off and slipped inside the photo.
explanation.definitionFit: A plastic surgeon performs skin grafts.

clue.text: Posers which may only trouble the 14 across? (7)

definitions.text: which may only trouble the 14 across?

blocks.note: a sitter poses for a portrait

blocks.clueFragment: which may only trouble the 14 across?
blocks.note: a sitter is an easy catch that only a butterfingered fielder would drop

explanation.surface: Awkward problems that bother only the clumsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posers' suggests puzzles; it is models. In cricket a sitter is a catch so easy that only a butterfingered player would miss it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitters pose for artists, and in cricket a sitter is a dolly catch.

clue.text: Come back to minister — can that be true? (7)

explanation.surface: Someone doubting news about a minister's return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' tempts toward politics; it is the clergy sense, giving REV.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: returning to a place or topic you have been to before.

clue.text: Famous printmaker saving a frame for painting (9)

indicators.note: save = except, so A is left out

explanation.surface: A celebrated engraver keeping a frame for a painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' seems to mean keeping; it means except, as in 'all save one'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretcher is the wooden frame a painting's canvas is stretched over.

clue.text: Certain that charges impress a felon (4)

indicators.note: to charge is to load, so these words hold the answer

explanation.surface: Criminal charges designed to make an impression on a lawbreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The courtroom surface hides the answer across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as in 'a safe bet', one sure to come off.

clue.text: Woolly you finally gave back after cycling (5)

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of you is used
giving something back returns it the way it came, so gave is read in reverse
then letters move round from the front to the back

explanation.surface: A complaint that after a bike ride you handed back something woolly.
explanation.walkthrough: U plus EVAG makes UEVAG; move the first two letters to the end and it becomes VAGUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolly is an idiom for fuzzy, muddled thinking that lacks a clear outline.

clue.text: Dark room with throne beneath Grand Mughal’s crown (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, LOO goes under G
the top, so the first letter

blocks.note: the throne is a jokey word for the toilet

explanation.surface: A gloomy chamber housing the throne of a great Mughal emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark room' looks like a photographer's darkroom; the definition is just 'Dark', and the room with a throne is a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Dark as a noun, the absence of light; the answer is partial darkness.

clue.text: Lie on thin bit of fabric (5)

explanation.surface: Lying down on a scrap of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie' reads as reclining; it is the untruth.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth is woven from threads, each spun from fine strands: those are the thin bits.

clue.text: Heavy load troubles European on motorway going around 100 mph (9)

indicators.note: in an across clue, placed after M
to go around something is to encircle it, so ILLS and E wrap round TON

blocks.note: doing a ton is driving at 100 mph

explanation.surface: A heavy lorry in trouble as a European driver speeds down the motorway at 100 mph.
explanation.walkthrough: British motorways are numbered M1, M25 and so on, hence M; a ton is slang for 100 mph.
explanation.definitionFit: A millstone round your neck is a heavy burden.

clue.text: Structure resisting great pressure from below cracked (3)

indicators.note: in a down clue, read from the bottom up

blocks.note: a dam holds back the weight of water

explanation.surface: An engineering note about a structure giving way under pressure from beneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracked' fits the engineering picture of a failing dam; it is the definition, meaning crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracked is informal slang for crazy, the mind likened to a broken pot.

clue.text: Revised dates agreed after loud festival (5,3)

indicators.note: changed, so the letters of dates are rearranged
the rearranged letters follow F

explanation.surface: Organisers agreeing new dates for a noisy festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loud festival' feels like one phrase; loud gives F and festival is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a saint's day or holy day in the church calendar, marked by celebration.

clue.text: Rate model making late start in occupation (5)

indicators.note: late is exchanged for another letter
the first letter of occupation

blocks.note: a template is a model to copy
first letter of occupation, put in LATE's place

explanation.surface: A price quoted for a model who is late starting a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making late start' looks like a tardy beginning; LATE in TEMPLATE is replaced by O.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is rate or speed, especially of music.
